query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The mechanical-property differences among the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEA and its quaternary/ternary subsets are governed primarily by variations in grain boundary segregation that lead to nanoclustering of key elements (notably Cr, Mn, and Ni), which in turn modifies grain boundary cohesion. By reducing the number of constituent elements, the segregation behavior is altered such that the embrittling effect at intermediate temperatures (400°C–800°C) is mitigated.
generation.material_initial_state: Annealed and recrystallized single-phase FCC alloys derived from the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system (and its quaternary and ternary subsets) obtained via identical thermomechanical processing.
generation.intervention: Systematically reduce the number of constituent elements (from the equiatomic quinary baseline to quaternary and then ternary alloys) while maintaining the same processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Tensile testing at a range of temperatures with a focus on intermediate temperatures (approximately 400°C to 800°C) where ductility loss has been observed, along with microstructural characterization during and after deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries affected by the degree and nature of elemental segregation and resultant nanoclustering.
generation.mechanism: During deformation at intermediate temperatures, certain principal elements (Cr, Mn, and Ni) rapidly segregate to grain boundaries. This nanoclustering locally reduces the cohesion of these boundaries and promotes cracking, leading to premature failure. In alloys with fewer elements (quaternary or ternary), the absence or reduction of one or more of these elements may alter the segregation dynamics, potentially reducing the embrittling effect at the GBs and thereby improving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary single-phase alloys will show a measurable difference in GB segregation behavior—observed as a reduction or alteration in the clustering of Cr, Mn, or Ni—resulting in less pronounced ductility loss and improved overall mechanical performance under intermediate temperature deformation.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloy, known to undergo fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni to grain boundaries during intermediate-temperature deformation that correlates with ductility loss.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to be valid only for single-phase FCC HEAs/MEAs produced by similar thermomechanical processing and operating under intermediate-temperature deformation conditions. It may not apply to alloys exhibiting multiphase structures or those with significant precipitate formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between constituent count reduction, segregation extent, and the resulting change in mechanical properties is not yet established. There is uncertainty regarding whether other deformation or microstructural mechanisms might also be influencing the property differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary single-phase FCC alloys using identical thermomechanical processing. Conduct tensile tests at intermediate temperatures (400°C–800°C) and use high-resolution microstructural characterization (e.g., atom probe tomography and electron microscopy) to quantify the degree of grain boundary segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Mn, and Ni. Correlate the mechanical performance (strength and ductility) of each alloy with its grain boundary chemistry.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves to record changes in strength and ductility
Atom probe tomography or equivalent to measure elemental segregation at grain boundaries
Fractography to assess the mode of failure (intergranular vs. transgranular cracking)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (a) reducing the number of constituent elements does not lead to a significant change in the segregation behavior or nanoclustering at grain boundaries compared to the equiatomic quinary alloy, or (b) no corresponding improvement in ductility or mechanical performance is observed. Additionally, if an alternative mechanism unrelated to grain boundary segregation is found to primarily dictate the ductility loss, the hypothesis would be deemed invalid.

## Abstract
Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

Here, we reveal the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss and provide guidelines for avoiding this problem.
The ductility loss in metals and alloys can be related to the segregation of impurity elements at GBs (, ) and the absorption of hydrogen or helium (), which weaken GB strength and promote crack initiation at GBs, and the precipitation of second phases (intermetallic compounds, carbides, nitrides, oxides, etc.) at GBs (, ), which causes high stress/strain concentration due to the incompatibility of elastic and plastic deformation between particles and matrix. These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.
